notes: First loop. I counted what a learner must hold at once. Step 1's 'short answer' shows three results plus a warning box with seven more numbers (report.txt:54-76) before step 2 introduces any input. Step 2 lists 17 inputs and 7 calculated figures (report.txt:106-277); 'What your numbers already say' gives no sentence saying what they mean. Step 3 bundles three ideas (versions, worst case, which guess matters), and every scenario card opens four 'working' rows, including 'Monthly result as a share of your fixed costs', which nothing later uses (report.txt:317-352). Step 4 promises 'the one number' and gives two (9 and 7, report.txt:441); the chart marks only 9 (src/report/charts.ts:267-271). The charts themselves teach well: zero line, words on the axes, readable at 390 px and in dark mode (report-phone.png, report-dark.png). The rehearsal grid misleads in small ways: Felix's 'Has lunch somewhere else' is drawn as 'Not around' (src/report/rehearsal.ts:50 matches 'elsewhere'), Rafael's 'Deal or not, this is my café' counts as engaged, and the real-customer checklist wears a 'Your number' chip (rehearsal.ts:230). The glossary comes after the terms are used (report.txt:896). The landing says seven steps; the report has six.
improvements: Step 1, src/report/sections.ts step1 (lines 106-112): cut the load before anything is taught. Keep one tile, the break-even, worded as a preview ('Step 4 works out how many extra lunch customers you need'), and move 'Worth knowing first' to the end of step 4 as 'Two things to notice', where 'pays its way' and switching regulars have just been explained. Why: one idea per step, no concept before it is introduced. Worked when step 1 on report-phone.png shows at most three numbers.

Step 3, src/report/sections.ts scenarioCard (lines 164-181): collapse 'The working' behind the existing 'Show the maths' pattern by default, drop 'Monthly result as a share of your fixed costs', and give the worst case and 'Which guess matters most' their own sub-heading ('How bad could it get, and which guess to test'), or move the second into step 6, where it explains what the test measures. Why: step 3 currently teaches three ideas with about 40 numbers. Worked when each scenario card shows its guess, its test result and one sentence by default.

Step 4, sections.ts step4 (lines 311-320) and charts.ts:267: name both break-evens. Label the 9 'pays back the test (incl. €180 setup)', add a second dashed marker at 7 'pays its way each day', retitle the step 'The numbers to remember', and add 'Pays its way' and 'Worst case' to GLOSSARY (sections.ts:437). Why: the chart and the text disagree on how many thresholds exist. Worked when the slider chart shows both markers and the slider at 8 lands visibly between them.

Rehearsal grid, src/report/rehearsal.ts:49-51 and :125: stop mapping 'elsewhere' to 'Not around'. Give it its own 'Went elsewhere' style; it is exactly the rival-offer effect the ⚡ event is meant to show. Count only actions that touch the deal as 'Engaged with the change' (Rafael's 'Keeps coming at lunchtime' is not), and replace chip('owner') on 'Check these with real customers' (line 230) with no chip or a plain 'To do' tag. Why: colour and labels are the lesson here; a mislabelled square or chip undoes the source-label teaching. Worked when Felix R2 reads 'Went elsewhere', round 4 shows 0 engaged, and no question carries 'Your number'.

Money format, test results in the tiles, scenario cards and slider readout (report.txt:61, 329, 481): round to whole euros (−€56, as cautious and optimistic already are). Then the worked example in 'Why this changed' reproduces by hand: 12.40 x 10 − 180 = −56 (report.txt:489 currently shows −€56.02). Why: a learner who checks the arithmetic and gets a different answer stops trusting 'Show the maths', and cents on a guess suggest certainty. Worked when every figure in the slider explanation matches its readout to the euro.

Point-of-use definitions and landing consistency: give the first use of 'break-even', 'worst case', 'pays its way' and 'takings' a tappable one-line definition (reuse the details/summary pattern of 'Why it matters'). On the landing, make site/index.html:87 'Seven small steps' match the report's six steps plus 'after the test', and redraw the step-3 mini chart and hero description (site/index.html:52, 108) so 'expected' can land on either side of zero. Why: a glossary at the end does not help while reading, and two step counts break the advance organiser. Worked when landing.txt and report.txt name the same steps and step 1 has tappable definitions.
misconceptionsRisked: 'Expected' means profit: the landing's mini chart and hero show 'expected' above break-even (site/index.html:52, 108), while the demo's likely guess loses €56.
Takings up means better: the cautious card shows '+€14.88 a day' change in takings next to '−€19.10 a day' result (report.txt:308-312) with no line explaining the gap.
Not around and went to a rival are the same thing: the grid hides the rival-offer effect (Felix R2).
Staying loyal is engaging with the deal: Rafael's square is green (report.txt:759).
A question to ask customers is 'your number': wrong chip on the checklist (report.txt:792-794).
Weekdays already lose money: €15,287 left after ingredients against €16,500 fixed costs with no caption (report.txt:238-248).
scaffoldingGaps: Step 1 previews results and introduces four concepts before step 2 lists a single number.
About 24 numbers in step 2 and about 40 in step 3 are visible at once on a phone; 'Show the maths' hides only the formulas, not the rows.
The glossary ('Five words', report.txt:896) is at the end and misses the terms the report actually uses: 'pays its way', 'pay back the test', 'worst case'.
The slider chart draws one break-even while the text teaches two.
'Why this changed' restates the arithmetic for the new position but never names the slope ('each extra customer a day adds €63 over the test'), which is the transferable mechanism.
Landing (seven steps) and report (six steps) give different maps of the same lesson.
